data_availability: Water-column chemistry, respiration rates, benthic flux measurements and sediment pore-water profiles are tabulated and plotted in the article. No separate data deposit.
caveat: One week of sampling (6–12 January 1994) in the dry season. The scanned PDF is OCR-degraded in places; check numeric values against the figures. The journal's DOI for this article does not resolve.

title: Global Bathymetry and Topography at 15 Arc Sec: SRTM15+
summary: The reference for what a 15 arc-second global grid actually is where no ship has been: depths predicted from satellite-altimeter gravity, not measured. It quantifies both the coverage and the penalty — only 10.84% of the ocean floor is constrained by shipboard soundings at 15 arc-second resolution, and altimetry-constrained cells carry uncertainties of ±150 to ±180 m. For a basin whose entire depth range is about 215 m, an altimetric prediction with ±180 m uncertainty near the coast carries no information at all. This is the quantitative basis for saying that a GEBCO or GMRT depth in Golfo Dulce is not a measurement.
verbatim_finding: Bathymetric grid cells constrained by satellite altimetry have estimated uncertainties of ±150 m in the deep oceans and ±180 m between coastlines and the continental rise.
data_availability: SRTM15+ grid distributed openly by Scripps Institution of Oceanography (topex.ucsd.edu) as netCDF; the paper documents the sounding and altimetry inputs. Open access.
caveat: Altimetric prediction is designed for the deep ocean; inside a 10-15 km wide gulf the gravity signal is dominated by the surrounding land and the method is not applicable, which the ±180 m near-coast figure understates rather than captures.

title: ADMIRALTY Chart 2493: Ports on the Pacific Coast of Costa Rica and Panama
summary: The British Admiralty's only coverage of the gulf, and it is coarser than the American one: Golfo Dulce appears as panel A of a three-panel plans chart at 1:100,000, sharing the sheet with Puerto Golfito (1:25,000) and two Panamanian ports. That the UKHO devotes a single 1:100,000 inset to a 50 km fjord with a 215 m anoxic basin — while giving four times that scale to the pier at Golfito — shows where hydrographic effort has historically gone: to berths and approaches, not to the basin. There is no larger-scale Admiralty coverage of the gulf interior.
verbatim_finding: A Costa Rica, Golfo Dulce 1:100,000 B Costa Rica, Puerto Golfito 1:25,000 C Panama, Puerto Armuelles and Charco Azul 1:25,000
data_availability: Commercial paper chart and ENC only; soundings are not distributed as data. Corrected to the latest Notices to Mariners by the agent at time of sale.
caveat: Edition date could not be established from an authoritative UKHO source without purchase, so the year is recorded as null rather than guessed. The panel scales are confirmed; the vintage of the underlying survey is not.

title: Characterization of some Golfo Dulce drainage basin rivers (Costa Rica)
summary: The baseline survey of the freshwater end-member feeding Golfo Dulce: 15 sites below 100 m altitude across the Osa Peninsula and the Esquinas and Coto Colorado basins, sampled through 1996–1997 for basic physicochemistry and benthic invertebrates. It is the source most directly relevant to quantifying what the rivers actually deliver — dissolved oxygen stayed within a narrow well-oxygenated range at every site, while suspended solids varied enormously between and within rivers with discharge, which is the variable that governs the sediment and turbidity plumes entering the gulf.
verbatim_finding: The rivers that drain into Golfo Dulce, south Pacific coast of Costa Rica, are important since they serve as vehicles of transport of materials and nutrients towards the gulf
data_availability: Site-by-site physicochemical measurements and species lists are tabulated in the article. No discharge time series and no digital deposit.
caveat: Spot sampling over two years, not gauged discharge. Gives concentrations, not loads — it cannot be used directly to compute freshwater or nutrient flux into the gulf. Scanned PDF is OCR-degraded.

title: Precolumbian Chiefdom Settlements with Stone Spheres of the Diquís
summary: The authoritative statement of what is protected and why in the Diquís Delta, immediately north-west of Golfo Dulce across the Osa peninsula. It fixes the serial property at four sites (Finca 6, Batambal, El Silencio, Grijalba-2), dates the chiefdom occupations to AD 500–1500, and gives the measured size range of the spheres (0.7–2.57 m). Crucially for a knowledge hub, it also states the preservation mechanism — burial under thick alluvial sediment shielded the spheres from the looting that stripped most Costa Rican sites — and flags the two development projects (Diquís hydroelectric dam, Southern International Airport) that were under discussion at inscription.
verbatim_finding: The four sites represent different settlement structures of chiefdom societies (500-1500 CE) containing artificial mounds, paved areas and burial sites.
data_availability: Statement of Outstanding Universal Value, criteria, integrity/authenticity assessments and management requirements as web text; linked document library gives the full nomination file (50 MB PDF), the 2014 ICOMOS advisory-body evaluation, property maps, and every State of Conservation report 2015–2025.
caveat: A conservation instrument, not a research paper: it summarises archaeological consensus rather than presenting primary excavation data, and the sphere chronology it endorses is broader than some site-specific datings.

title: From seamount accretion to tectonic erosion: Formation of Osa Mélange and the effects of Cocos Ridge subduction in southern Costa Rica
summary: Explains why the rocks around Golfo Dulce are exposed at all. The Osa Peninsula is a window into the outer forearc: a middle Eocene–middle Miocene mélange of basalt, chert and limestone built by seamount accretion, exhumed when the Middle America Trench switched from accretion to severe tectonic erosion at the Miocene–Pliocene boundary as thickened Galápagos-derived crust (the palaeo-Cocos Ridge) arrived at the trench. Critically for the shape of the gulf, the paper shows the change from accretion to erosion fragmented the outer forearc along subvertical faults into kilometre- to tens-of-kilometre-scale blocks undergoing differential vertical motion in response to the morphology of the subducting ridge — the structural grain within which the Golfo Dulce depression sits.
verbatim_finding: The thick crust caused uplift and severe tectonic erosion of the accretionary edifice allowing exhumation of the Osa Mélange.
data_availability: Structural mapping, mélange fabric analysis and biostratigraphic constraints presented in the paper. No deposited dataset. Wiley paywall.
caveat: The interpretation drew a formal published Comment from Buchs & Baumgartner (10.1029/2006tc002032), who argue much of what Vannucchi et al. map as mélange is coherent accreted igneous crust; see the authors' Reply (10.1029/2007tc002129). A Correction also exists (10.1029/2006tc002013).

title: Flatfish (Pleuronectiformes) species richness and depth distribution in the Gulf of Nicoya, Golfo Dulce, and two adjacent areas on the Pacific coast of Costa Rica
summary: A synthesis of four decades of trawl surveys (Skimmer 1979–1989, Nishin Maru 1987–1988, Victor Hensen 1993–1994) that is one of the few papers to connect a whole demersal fish group directly to the oxygen structure of the water column. Thirty-six flatfish species were found over 8–359 m; 19 of them occur in Golfo Dulce between 20 and 235 m, and the authors state plainly that 58 % of species were taken below 100 m and were therefore probably living under hypoxia. Cluster analysis shows low similarity between stations, implying habitat partitioning. The paper also supplies 2000–2016 semi-industrial landings figures showing flatfish are under 1 % of landings, and notes the post-2014 collapse in trawler numbers as an opportunity to update the gulf's trophic models.
verbatim_finding: A total of 21 species (58 %) were found at depths greater than 100 m and were probably exposed the low oxygen concentrations characteristic of hypoxia.
data_availability: Assembled species-by-depth list drawn from published survey lists and Museo de Zoología UCR specimens; landings series 2000–2016 for the semi-industrial fleet included in the open-access article.
caveat: Historical trawl records with unequal effort across surveys and decades; hypoxic exposure is inferred from depth rather than measured at capture.

title: A fjord-like tropical ecosystem, Pacific coast of Costa Rica: overview of research in Golfo Dulce
summary: The definitive review of Golfo Dulce research, synthesising 123 studies and organising them around the vertical oxygen and temperature profiles that structure the system. It is the single best source for the central ecological claim of this topic: the gulf is hypoxic below about 50 m and frequently anoxic in the 200 m inner basin with occasional H2S, yet it nevertheless supports high diversity from bacteria to whales. The authors identify what is still missing — primary productivity, biomass of the main planktonic, demersal and benthic groups, and the frequency and magnitude of deep offshore water spilling over the sill — and argue these are needed to update the trophic model built more than 25 years earlier from the R/V Victor Hensen expedition.
verbatim_finding: Golfo Dulce has low oxygen concentrations below 50 m and is frequently anoxic at the 200 m deep basin with occasional formation of H2S.
data_availability: No new data; a curated synthesis with full bibliography of 123 Golfo Dulce studies, open access under CC-BY. A companion reference list is maintained by CIMAR at cimar.ucr.ac.cr.
caveat: A review, not primary measurement: the oxygen figures are drawn from the underlying studies (notably Córdoba & Vargas 1996, Ferdelman et al. 2006), and the depth of the hypoxic boundary varies between surveys and with sill-overflow events.

title: Percepción comunitaria sobre arrecifes coralinos en Golfo Dulce: bases para integración social en programas de restauración
summary: 183 structured interviews (2016–2017) with artisanal fishers, tourism operators and other residents around Golfo Dulce, measuring both factual knowledge of coral reefs and perceptions of threat and management. The findings are directly usable for a public knowledge hub: tourism workers were the best-informed group (42 % 'informed'), a third of the general public was uninformed, and over 60 % of both fishers and tourism operators independently named sedimentation and agrochemical contamination as the principal threat — the same two stressors the biophysical literature identifies. Sixty per cent expect the gulf's marine resources to be worse in future; visitation restrictions were the least accepted management measure, permanent mooring buoys the most.
verbatim_finding: Sedimentation and contamination by agrochemicals were identified by more than 60 % of PA and T as the main threat.
data_availability: Interview responses summarised by stakeholder group and perception scale in the open-access article; raw questionnaires not deposited.
caveat: Social-perception data, not ecological measurement; convenience sampling of coastal communities and a 2016–2017 snapshot.

title: A carbonate platform associated with shallow cold methane seeps in Golfo Dulce, Pacific Costa Rica
container: Galaxea, Journal of Coral Reef Studies
summary: First report of a cold methane seep in shallow, warm, oxygen-saturated tropical water — a combination previously unknown outside hydrothermal settings. At 10 m depth the authors found a ~100 m2 carbonate platform standing ~2 m above mud, venting odourless high-methane gas, with pore water inside the platform at 5 µM O2 down to below detection while the overlying column was 97–100% saturated. Carbon isotope signatures of the crust point to authigenic carbonate formed by anaerobic oxidation of methane. It establishes that Golfo Dulce's methane story is not confined to the deep anoxic basin: there is a shallow geological methane source too.

data_availability: Photogallery-format note. Gas composition, O2 microsensor readings and stable carbon isotope values are reported in the text; underwater photographs are the primary figures. No data deposit.
caveat: A short 'Photogallery' contribution, not a full research paper — findings are described as preliminary by the authors. Superseded in detail by Salas et al. (2023).

title: Abundancia, reproducción y tallas del tiburón martillo Sphyrna lewini (Carcharhiniformes: Sphyrnidae) en la pesca artesanal de Golfo Dulce, Pacífico de Costa Rica
summary: The paper that established Golfo Dulce as a nursery area for the critically endangered scalloped hammerhead and converted that into a specific, actionable management proposal. All 315 hammerheads sampled from artisanal trips were juveniles, averaging 74.3 cm total length, and mean size moved inversely to catch rate — smallest animals taken when CPUE was highest, in July-August. On that basis the authors recommend seasonal closures during the June-August pupping window at the specific sites where catches concentrate. This is the clearest example in the literature of a Golfo Dulce study designed to feed directly into INCOPESCA regulation.
verbatim_finding: Se analizaron un total de 315 tiburones, todos juveniles, con una longitud total media de 74.3±17.4cm.
data_availability: Length-frequency distributions, sex ratios and monthly CPUE are published in the article. Open access; no separate data deposit.
caveat: Fishery-dependent sampling over a single year, so abundance trends cannot be separated from changes in fishing effort or gear deployment.
